decisions.quote: Apart from arising in response to physical stressors, freezing can also occur in response to social threats. Specifically, Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins ( 2010 ) showed freezing in response to angry faces, suggesting that freezing is a generic threat response (see also Hagenaars et al., 2014a , b ). This is important because freezing in response to social situations has several practical implications ranging from the treatment of psychological trauma (Kozlowska, Walker, McLean, & Carrive, 2015 ) to improving the quality of social interactions (Mendes, Blascovich, Hunter, Lickel, & Jost, 2007 ). Given the important theoretical and practical consequences of freezing in response to social stress, together with the fact that Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ) is the only study showing freezing in response to social threat, the current study aimed to replicate Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ).
decisions.reason: Shipped row 2009 and blind target_index 0 both correctly identify the replicated original study as Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins (2010), 'Facing freeze: Social threat induces bodily freeze in humans' (Psychological Science, 21, 1575-1581; DOI: 10.1177/0956797610384746). Row 2009 was only left unpaired in the follow-up snapshot because shipped row 422 was a duplicate entry for the same replication that originally had erroneous metadata and was resolved to target_index 0 in the prior round.

decisions.quote: Like Roelofs et al. we find that the block effects are modulated by state anxiety, although only when excluding a STAI outlier. The fact that we only find this modulation when excluding an STAI outlier might suggest that the effects are not extremely reliable, as individual data-points can then have a substantial influence on effects. Indeed, in our study, the effect is marginal and we do not replicate the negative correlation between heart rate and STAI in the angry block. While our findings are not completely in line with Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ), they support the notion that people show physiological signs of freezing in response to social threat.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly designed Step 1 of their replication to re-test both whether viewing angry faces lowers heart rate relative to neutral/happy faces and whether this effect relates to state anxiety as in Roelofs et al. (2010). While they confirmed lower heart rate in the angry block (with marginal state-anxiety modulation only after excluding a STAI outlier), they explicitly state in the Abstract, Results, and Discussion that 'we do not replicate the negative correlation between heart rate and STAI in the angry block' and summarize in the Discussion that 'While our findings are not completely in line with Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ), they support the notion that people show physiological signs of freezing in response to social threat.' Addressing the blind coder's objection that the concluding sentence ('To conclude, the current research has largely replicated the freezing-to-social-threat effect initially demonstrated by Roelofs et al. ( 2010 )') is an overriding overall verdict for 'successful': that sentence specifically refers to the main 'freezing-to-social-threat effect' and qualifies it as 'largely replicated' because of the un-replicated STAI correlation. Under the codebook, confirming one tested effect does not override an explicit statement that the study did not replicate another tested original finding ('a tested finding the paper itself contrasts with the original may not' be omitted, and stating 'we do not replicate...' alongside a confirmed finding yields 'mixed').

decisions.quote: Given the important theoretical and practical consequences of freezing in response to social stress, together with the fact that Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ) is the only study showing freezing in response to social threat, the current study aimed to replicate Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ).
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 2009 and blind coding classify the record as a replication. The study collected new heart-rate and state-anxiety data from an independent sample of 60 Dutch student participants (final N = 54) to re-test the findings of Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins (2010).
